evidence.claim: Idaho 28 follows the Lemhi Valley between Salmon and the highway junction near Mud Lake.
evidence.quote: state highway in Idaho which runs from Idaho State Highway 33 (SH-33) near Mud Lake to U.S. Route 93 in Salmon.

evidence.claim: Between Salmon and Leadore, the road runs beside the Lemhi River for several miles.
evidence.quote: Just after exiting the town, the road travels parallel to the Lemhi River for several miles before ending at U.S. Route 93 in the community of Salmon.

evidence.claim: Sacajawea was born in the Lemhi Valley near Salmon.
evidence.quote: Sacagawea, was born in the Lemhi Valley near Salmon.

evidence.claim: The Lewis and Clark Expedition crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass and followed the Salmon River through the site of the present city.
evidence.quote: The Lewis and Clark Expedition crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass, 30 miles (48 km) to the southeast of Salmon. They followed the Salmon River through the present site of the city

evidence.claim: A later transport connection linked the valley’s towns: from 1910 to 1939, Salmon was the western terminus of the Gilmore and Pittsburgh Railroad.
evidence.quote: From 1910 to 1939, Salmon was the western terminus of the now-defunct Gilmore and Pittsburgh Railroad.

evidence.claim: Traveling southeast from Salmon, Idaho 28 passes through Lemhi and then Leadore, where it meets Idaho 29.
evidence.quote: Lemhi is located along Idaho State Highway 28 and the Lemhi River, 8 miles (13 km) south of Tendoy and 18 miles (29 km) northwest of Leadore.

evidence.claim: Traveling southeast from Salmon, Idaho 28 passes through Lemhi and then Leadore, where it meets Idaho 29.
evidence.quote: The roadway passes the Leadore Airport on its way into Leadore, meeting Idaho State Highway 29 while in the community.

evidence.claim: The highway continues toward Mud Lake and its junction with Idaho 33.
evidence.quote: Idaho State Highway 28 begins at an intersection with ID 33. The route heads northwest before passing the Mud Lake Airport

evidence.quote: Sacagawea, was born in the Lemhi Valley near Salmon. The Sacajawea Interpretive, Cultural and Educational Center was opened in Salmon in August 2003.

evidence.claim: The center interprets the Salmon and Lemhi River country, including Sacajawea, her people and the Lewis and Clark Expedition.
evidence.quote: which was shaped in part by the Lewis and Clark Expedition and Sacajawea, as well as her people, the Agai’dika Shoshone-Bannock Tribes.

evidence.claim: The center interprets the Salmon and Lemhi River country, including Sacajawea, her people and the Lewis and Clark Expedition.
evidence.quote: interprets the rich cultural and natural history of the Salmon and Lemhi River Country

evidence.claim: Its 71 acres adjoin the Lemhi River and include outdoor trails, community gardens and a research library.
evidence.quote: Located on 71 acres abutting the Lemhi River, the Sacajawea Center has a visitor center & gift shop, outdoor amphitheater, community gardens, miles of outdoor trails, a research library

evidence.claim: The expedition crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass, southeast of Salmon, before following the Salmon River through the present city and turning north toward Montana.
evidence.quote: The Lewis and Clark Expedition crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass, 30 miles (48 km) to the southeast of Salmon. They followed the Salmon River through the present site of the city, then ascended the north fork of the river

evidence.claim: Leadore’s community center is a railway-station replica, built in 2001.
evidence.quote: In 2001 a replica of the town's old railway station was constructed in Leadore. The new building serves as the town's community center.

evidence.claim: The town dates from 1910, when the Gilmore and Pittsburgh Railroad crossed Bannock Pass into the Lemhi Valley.
evidence.quote: The town of Leadore dates from 1910, when the Gilmore and Pittsburgh Railroad was constructed from Armstead, Montana, over Bannock Pass and into the Lemhi Valley.

evidence.claim: The intended station site at Junction changed because its landowner refused to sell.
evidence.quote: the original location for the train station in the town of Junction had to be altered when the owner of the land refused to sell.

evidence.claim: Leadore housed the repair shops and the junction of the Gilmore branch with the main line.
evidence.quote: The town was home to the railroad's repair shops, and was the point where the railroad's branch line to Gilmore connected with the main line.

evidence.claim: The railroad stopped operating in 1939.
evidence.quote: the railroad ceased operating in 1939

evidence.claim: Idaho 28 now passes through town as Railroad Street.
evidence.quote: Idaho State Highway 28 (Railroad Street) passes through the center of Leadore

evidence.claim: The Lemhi River crosses the northeast side of Leadore, flowing northwest to meet the Salmon River at Salmon.
evidence.quote: The Lemhi River flows through the northeast side of the city, running northwest to join the Salmon River at Salmon, Idaho.

evidence.claim: Four kiln ruins survive from a group of sixteen built in 1886 to fuel the Nicholia smelter.
evidence.quote: The kilns were built in 1886 to produce charcoal to fuel the smelter at Nicholia

evidence.claim: Four kiln ruins survive from a group of sixteen built in 1886 to fuel the Nicholia smelter.
evidence.quote: The ruins of four kilns survive.

evidence.claim: Warren King built them with bricks made from local clay.
evidence.quote: A Butte, Montana, man named Warren King built 16 kilns from brick made from local clay

evidence.claim: Each beehive-shaped kiln measured about 20 feet tall and 20 feet across.
evidence.quote: The beehive-shaped kilns are each about 20 feet (6.1 m) tall and 20 feet (6.1 m) in diameter.

evidence.claim: The operation lasted less than three years.
evidence.quote: The kiln operation lasted for less than three years

evidence.claim: A volunteer-assisted stabilization saved one kiln from collapse in 1987, and the Forest Service restored the kilns in 2000.
evidence.quote: In 1987, a volunteer-assisted stabilization effort prevented one of the kilns from collapsing. The Forest Service undertook a restoration of the kilns in 2000.

evidence.claim: Nothing survives of Woodland, the nearby settlement where kiln workers lived.
evidence.quote: There are no surviving remains of the town of Woodland, a short distance south of the kilns, where the kiln workers lived.

evidence.claim: Each kiln consumed 30 to 40 cords of Douglas fir per load, burning for two days to produce charcoal.
evidence.quote: When operating, each kiln used 30 to 40 cords of Douglas fir wood per load, producing about 1,500 to 2,000 bushels (70 cubic meters) of charcoal over a two-day burn.

flags: Cache lacks byway-body interpretation, road construction history, driving time and much of the physical description. Overview uses documented valley transport history; it does not identify expedition or railroad alignments with the modern road.

Dropped unsupported current claims: mostly straight road, almost 100 miles beside the Divide, Gilmore Summit elevation and low-pass description, 1805 horse-and-guide negotiations, salmon-eaters translation, seasonal advice, and center trail displays of a tipi camp, sweat lodge and fish weir.

Sources use Sacagawea and Sacajawea, and Lemhi Shoshone versus Agai’dika Shoshone-Bannock Tribes; kept the byway and center spelling, omitted unsupported equivalences. No Tribal primary source is cached.
Strip mileage runs from Salmon southeast, the reverse of the current draft; moments follow that direction. Kilns are a separate excursion, not a promised roadside stop.
Material and highway page disagree on mileage and corridor extent. Omitted mileage and I-15 approach designation rather than treating catalog data as evidence.
